summary: Describes conventions for using several cryptographic algorithms with the CMS encrypted key package content type, covering the EnvelopedData, EncryptedData, and AuthEnvelopedData structures.

plainLanguage.summary: When one key is wrapped inside another for transport, the two sides must agree on which ciphers and signature methods to use. This document lists the required and recommended choices, and adds no new methods of its own.

subtitle: Which encryption, key management and signature algorithms to support when protecting cryptographic keys in CMS.

tldr.problem: The CMS encrypted key package content type needs agreed algorithm choices so implementations interoperate when carrying cryptographic keys.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets MUST and SHOULD algorithms for EnvelopedData, EncryptedData, AuthEnvelopedData and SignedData, led by AES Key Wrap with Padding. It defines no new algorithms.
tldr.outcome: Conforming implementations share a baseline of AES-128 key wrap, RSA and SHA-256, with public keys of 1024 to 2048 bits. The unit metadata says RFC 6161 updates this document.

today: RFC 6033 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists RFC 6161 as updating it, and no RFC as obsoleting it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 6033 gives conventions for using cryptographic algorithms with the CMS encrypted key package content type from RFC 6032. It covers EnvelopedData and EncryptedData (RFC 5652) and AuthEnvelopedData (RFC 5083), and it also gives requirements for SignedData and public key sizes.

The document defines no new algorithms; it refers to algorithms defined elsewhere and marks each one required (MUST), recommended (SHOULD) or optional (MAY).
sections.plainLanguage: This is a list of approved methods for wrapping and signing keys. Some are required, some are recommended and some are optional, and the document borrows all of them from other specifications.

sections.title: EnvelopedData and EncryptedData
sections.content:
For EnvelopedData, implementations that claim conformance MUST support the key transport mechanisms and SHOULD support key agreement. With key transport, RSA encryption MUST be supported and RSAES-OAEP SHOULD be. With key agreement, Ephemeral-Static Diffie-Hellman MUST be supported.

Whatever key management is chosen, implementations MUST support AES-128 Key Wrap with Padding as the content-encryption algorithm, and SHOULD support AES-256 Key Wrap with Padding. When key agreement is used, the key wrap algorithm must match the AES size of the content-encryption algorithm. EncryptedData leaves key management to other means, so only the content-encryption algorithm is specified, with the same MUST and SHOULD.
sections.plainLanguage: The wrapped content uses a key-only encryption method. AES-128 key wrap is required and AES-256 is recommended, and if key agreement is used the two sizes must match.

sections.title: AuthEnvelopedData and SignedData
sections.content:
AuthEnvelopedData has the same key management requirements as EnvelopedData; the difference is the content-encryption algorithm. Implementations MUST support 128-bit AES-GCM and SHOULD support 256-bit AES-GCM. They MAY also support AES-CCM.

For SignedData, implementations MUST support the signature scheme RSA and SHOULD support RSASSA-PSS and DSA. Together with these signature schemes, implementations MUST support the hash function SHA-256 and SHOULD support SHA-1.
sections.plainLanguage: The authenticated form adds a tamper check on top of the encryption, and it requires the AES-GCM mode. Signed data needs RSA signatures plus the SHA-256 hash, with a few optional extras.

sections.title: Key Sizes and Security Considerations
sections.content:
If an implementation supports RSA, RSAES-OAEP, Diffie-Hellman, RSASSA-PSS or DSA, it MUST support key lengths from 1024 bits to 2048 bits, inclusive.

The security considerations of the referenced algorithm documents apply. The choice of content-encryption algorithm follows RFC 5649, which favours a mechanism used only to protect keying material so that keys can be kept apart from other data. The RFC notes that no AES-GCM or AES-CCM mode provides that property, and says the document will be updated if one is defined.
sections.plainLanguage: Public keys may be 1024 to 2048 bits long. The key-only wrapping method is preferred because it keeps keys separate from ordinary data, and no authenticated mode offers the same benefit yet.
